rakomelo: Rakomelo is named for its two parts, raki and meli, the Greek word for honey. In Crete the raki is tsikoudia, the clear spirit distilled each autumn from the grape skins and pips left after winemaking, and warming it with honey and cinnamon, sometimes clove, is a household winter habit with no credited inventor. It is also sold ready-made, and a spicier relative, psimeni raki, is the speciality of the island of Amorgos. In Cretan tavernas a small carafe of raki often arrives unasked after a meal, and in winter it may come as rakomelo.
ponche-de-frutas: Guatemala's ponche de frutas belongs to Christmas, to the posadas, the neighbourhood processions of the days before it, and to the family dinner of Nochebuena. Its name comes, by way of Spanish, from the English word punch, and it is a close cousin of Mexico's ponche navideño. No one is credited with a first recipe; each household settles its own mix of fruit such as pineapple, papaya, apple, raisins and prunes, simmered with cinnamon and sugar, and rum is added at the table, if at all, with the fruit eaten by spoon.
kremas: Kremas, also written crémas or crémasse, is the Haitian drink of the Christmas and New Year season, made at home in large batches from cream of coconut, condensed milk, rum, vanilla, lime and spice. Barbancourt rhum is the usual choice today, though clairin, Haiti's own cane spirit, has long gone into it too. No one is credited with the first recipe, and families in Haiti and across the diaspora each keep their own, varying the spice and sometimes adding fruit.
guifiti: Gifiti, also spelled guifiti, is the rum bitters of the Garífuna, whose ancestors were deported by the British from St Vincent at the end of the eighteenth century and settled along the Caribbean coast of Honduras, Belize, Guatemala and Nicaragua. It began as a household preparation, rum steeped with roots, barks, herbs, garlic and spice until it turns green or brown, with recipes kept in families and differing from village to village. It is now also bottled commercially, among others by Travellers Liquors of Belize.
froccs: The best-known story of fröccs is set on 5 October 1842 in András Fáy's wine cellar at Fót, where Ányos Jedlik, the Benedictine physicist who pioneered soda water in Hungary, mixed wine with his sparkling water and called it spriccer. The poet Mihály Vörösmarty, one of the guests, is said to have disliked the German word and coined fröccs, from the Hungarian for a splash. Hungarians were already mixing wine with naturally sparkling spring water before then, and the ratios now have names of their own, from kisfröccs, one part wine to one of soda, to házmester, three to two.
puszta-cocktail: The Puszta Cocktail joins two Hungarian staples, apricot brandy and Unicum, with dry vermouth under the name of the Great Hungarian Plain, and no bar or bartender has a recorded claim to it.
brennivin-og-appelsin: Brennivín with Appelsín, Iceland's caraway schnapps lengthened with the country's own orange soda, is an informal Icelandic mix that nobody is recorded as having invented.
old-monk-and-cola: Old Monk with cola and a squeeze of lime is India's everyday way with its best-known dark rum, a pairing that no one is credited with and that has no recorded first glass.
urrak-with-limca: Urrak, the light first distillate of Goa's cashew season, is lengthened with lemon soda such as Limca, a pinch of salt and a green chilli as a local summer habit with no recorded inventor.
arak-madu: Arak madu simply means arak with honey, a plain Balinese serve of the island's village-distilled arak with honey and lime that no bar or maker is credited with.
hot-whiskey: In Ireland the hot toddy goes by a plainer name, hot whiskey or a hot Irish: whiskey, sugar and boiling water with a slice of lemon studded with cloves. The word toddy came from India, where it meant fermented palm sap, and by the late eighteenth century the British used it for spirits mixed with hot water, sugar and spice. No one is credited with the Irish version, made at home and in pubs through the winter, where the boiling water is often poured over a metal spoon standing in the glass to spare the glass some of the heat.
irish-flag: The Irish Flag is a layered shot built in the green, white and orange of the Irish tricolour, one of many flag-coloured shots poured for national days, and nobody has recorded who first made it.
arak-grapefruit: Arak with grapefruit juice over crushed ice is one of Israel's everyday long drinks, pairing the Levant's anise spirit with local citrus, and no bar or bartender is credited with it.
barbajada: The barbajada carries the name of Domenico Barbaja, who began as a café waiter in Milan and is credited with inventing this frothy whip of chocolate, coffee, milk and sugar, served cold in summer and hot under cream in winter. It helped make his first fortune before he became one of the great opera impresarios of his age, running the Teatro San Carlo in Naples, where he put Rossini under contract. An early nineteenth-century account of Sardinia records the exiled King Victor Emmanuel I taking it at breakfast every day, and it stayed popular in Milan's cafés well into the twentieth century.
barracuda: The Barracuda is credited to Benito Cuppari, a bartender from Genoa who was head bartender aboard the Italian liner Michelangelo when he created it in the late 1960s and won a bartending competition with it. Its build sets rum and pineapple beside two Italian ingredients, Galliano and a top of prosecco, and why Cuppari named it after the fish is not recorded. The International Bartenders Association later listed it among its New Era drinks before dropping it again.
bicicletta: The Bicicletta is a Lombard bar habit rather than an invention with a date: Campari with still white wine and a splash of soda, a light afternoon order in the towns of northern Italy. The usual explanation of the name points to the older regulars who rode to the bar by bicycle and pedalled home afterwards, a story that is told rather than documented, and nobody is credited with the first glass.
caffe-corretto: Corretto means corrected, and in Italian bars a caffè corretto is an espresso corrected with a little spirit, most often grappa, sometimes sambuca or brandy. Nobody is credited with the idea, which grew out of everyday bar habit, and it has cousins elsewhere, the carajillo in Spain and karsk in Norway among them. Some bars add the spirit to the cup and others bring it in its own small glass, and in the Veneto the resentin, from the dialect for rinsing, is a splash of spirit swirled round the empty cup.
milano-torino: The Milano-Torino takes its name from its two halves, bitter from Milan and sweet vermouth from Turin, and in Italy it is often ordered by its short name, MiTo. It is often traced to the Milan of Gaspare Campari in the later nineteenth century, but there is no firm evidence of who first mixed it. Its family tree is clearer: lengthened with soda it becomes the Americano, and with gin added it becomes the Negroni.
rossini: The Rossini is one of a family of prosecco drinks modelled on the Bellini, the white peach and prosecco cocktail created by Giuseppe Cipriani at Harry's Bar in Venice. Swapping the peach for fresh strawberry purée gave the Rossini, named after the composer Gioachino Rossini, and other members of the family took artists' names too, among them the Tintoretto, made with pomegranate. Who first poured the Rossini, and when, is not recorded.
ve-n-to: The Ve.n.to is credited to two Italian bartenders, Samuele Ambrosi and Leonardo Veronesi, working with Grappa Revolution, a project founded by Leonardo Pinto to bring grappa into modern cocktails. They built it on the old pairing of grappa and honey, with lemon and chamomile, and its name is drawn from Veneto and Trentino, two regions closely tied to grappa. With the backing of Giorgio Fadda, then president of the International Bartenders Association, it became the first grappa cocktail on the IBA's official list.
bob-marley: The Bob Marley is a layered shot built in the red, gold and green associated with the Jamaican singer and with reggae, and no one has recorded who first poured it or where.
dirty-banana: The Dirty Banana is a blended Jamaican resort drink of banana, cream, rum and coffee liqueur, often the island's own Tia Maria, and no bar has a documented claim to the first one.
planters-punch: Punch reached the Caribbean with British sailors and traders, and Jamaica's planter's punch is its best-known descendant. The earliest known printed recipe is a verse in the London magazine Fun in September 1878, set in Jamaica, and the familiar rhyme of one of sour, two of sweet, three of strong and four of weak was printed in The New York Times in 1908. No individual is credited with the drink, which is on the International Bartenders Association's list of official cocktails.
ting-with-a-sting: Ting with a sting is simply Jamaica's grapefruit soda Ting with rum in it, often the island's white overproof, a rum-shop order that no one is credited with naming or first pouring.
bamboo: Japanese cocktail histories date the dry Bamboo to around 1890 and credit Louis Eppinger, a hotel man who had tended bar in San Francisco before coming to Yokohama in 1889 to run the Grand Hotel. The name is older than his version: American newspapers in 1886 reported a fashionable new drink called the Bamboo in New York bars, made with sherry and sweet vermouth. Eppinger seems to have reworked it with dry vermouth, William Boothby printed that version under his name in 1908, and in Japan it is counted among Yokohama's four classic cocktails.
lemon-sour: Lemon sour grew out of the chūhai, short for shōchū highball, the shochu-and-soda drinks usually traced to the izakaya of Tokyo's working districts after the Second World War, where soda made plain shochu easier to enjoy. In Japan a sour means a spirit with citrus and soda rather than the shaken American drink, and lemon became the flavour most people order, though no single bar is credited with the first. Many izakaya now serve a fresh version with half a lemon and a hand squeezer, so guests press their own juice into the glass.
million-dollar: Japanese accounts credit the Million Dollar to Louis Eppinger, who ran Yokohama's Grand Hotel in the 1890s and is also credited with the dry Bamboo, though a dry-gin version is linked to the Raffles Hotel in Singapore. Shōgo Hamada, who trained under Eppinger, carried it to Tokyo, and when the 1923 earthquake closed the Tokyo Kaikan he moved to Café Lion in Ginza, where it became a great favourite. The writer Kikuchi Kan, a regular, named it in a 1926 advertisement as the cocktail among cocktails, just as his Bungei Shunjū was the magazine among magazines.
umeshu-soda: Umeshu soda lengthens Japan's plum liqueur, unripe ume steeped in shochu with sugar, with soda over ice, one of the standard ways it is ordered in Japan, and the serve has no recorded inventor.
kumys: Kumys belongs to the horse peoples of the Central Asian steppe, Kazakhs, Kyrgyz, Bashkirs and Mongols among them, and it is very old. Herodotus described the Scythians processing mare's milk, the Turkic word kımız was written down in the eleventh century, and the Franciscan traveller William of Rubruck described the Mongols making what he called cosmos in the thirteenth. Because mare's milk is scarce, much commercial kumys is now made from cow's milk.
dawa: Dawa takes its Swahili name, medicine, in jest: it is vodka, lime and honey crushed over ice, a close cousin of the caipiroska. It is often linked to the Carnivore restaurant in Nairobi, where it was served to visitors and became something of a Kenyan signature, though who first made it is not recorded. Its distinctive tool is the dawa stick, a muddler coated in honey that stays in the glass, so each drinker stirs in sweetness to taste.
black-balsam-and-blackcurrant: Riga Black Balsam stirred into hot blackcurrant juice is one of the commonest Latvian ways to serve the herbal balsam in winter, a household pairing that no one is credited with.
riga-black-magic: Riga Black Magic is a modern Latvian mix of Riga Black Balsam with apple juice, lemon and a little sugar, and no bar or bartender has published a claim to it or to its name.
arak-lemonade: Arak with mint lemonade is an informal Lebanese way of turning the anise spirit into a long summer drink, a habit that no one is credited with and that has no recorded origin.
planteur: The planteur is the French Antilles' take on planter's punch, and it takes its name from the planters of the cane estates. What sets it apart is the rum: in Martinique and Guadeloupe that usually means rhum agricole, distilled from fresh cane juice rather than molasses, a style that spread on the islands in the late nineteenth century after a collapse in sugar prices. Recipes differ from bar to bar and family to family, mixing the rum with tropical juices and cane syrup, and no one is credited with the first.
cazuela: The cazuela is a Mexican tequila punch named for the wide clay pot it is served in, packed with citrus, ice and grapefruit soda and shared through straws, and no one has documented who first mixed one.
charro-negro: The charro negro is a Mexican highball of blanco tequila, cola and lime, and neither its inventor nor the story behind its name is recorded.
chelada: Chela is Mexican slang for a beer, and the chelada is the plainest of the country's prepared beers: lager over ice with lime juice in a salt-rimmed glass. The name of its spicier relative, the michelada, has two explanations, one crediting Michel Ésper of the Club Deportivo Potosino in San Luis Potosí, whose beer with lime and salt other members ordered as Michel's limonada, the other reading it as mi chela helada, my cold beer. Names shift by region, and what one city calls a chelada another may call a michelada.
la-bandera: La bandera, the flag, is a way of serving tequila rather than a mixed drink: three small glasses side by side of green lime juice, white blanco tequila and red sangrita, the colours of the Mexican flag. Sangrita comes from Jalisco and is usually traced to Guadalajara and Lake Chapala, where the leftover juices of an orange-and-chilli fruit salad were sipped alongside tequila, its red coming from chilli and pomegranate rather than tomato. No one is credited with arranging the three glasses into a flag.
mexican-firing-squad: The Mexican Firing Squad comes to us through Charles H. Baker Jr., the American writer who collected drinks on his travels and recorded this one at La Cucaracha bar in Mexico City in 1937. He printed it in The Gentleman's Companion of 1939, which makes it one of the earlier tequila cocktails in English print, but he did not record who created it or why it carries its stark name. The short recipe, tequila with lime, grenadine and Angostura, returned to menus when bartenders began mining Baker's books for forgotten drinks.
mezcalita: The mezcalita is the margarita remade with Oaxaca's smoky mezcal, a swap that rose with mezcal's own popularity and that no bartender is credited with first making.
submarino: The submarino takes its name from the shot glass of tequila that sinks, glass and all, to the bottom of a light lager, a Mexican party serve with no recorded inventor.
torito: The torito, little bull, is a drink of Veracruz on the Gulf coast: cane aguardiente blended with condensed and evaporated milk and a flavouring, classically peanut but also guanábana, mango or coconut. Local accounts trace it to the cane plantations of the Papaloapan basin, where workers mixed their aguardiente with seasonal fruit, though no one is credited with the recipe. In Morelos and the State of Mexico the same name belongs to a quite different drink, made with orange juice, onion and pickled chillies.
vampiro: The vampiro is a tequila highball from Jalisco, built with tequila, grapefruit soda, lime and sangrita, the chilli-and-citrus juice the region sips alongside tequila, and the red of the sangrita is the usual explanation for its name. No one has documented who first mixed it. Bottled sangrita became a common shortcut, though purists still make it fresh, and the International Bartenders Association listed the vampiro among its New Era drinks before dropping it from the list.
airag: Airag is the Mongolian name for fermented mare's milk, the drink known further west as kumys, and it is made each summer while the mares are in milk. Fresh milk is poured into a leather bag or wooden vessel with some of the previous batch and churned or stirred over hours or days, so that it sours and takes on a gentle fizz. The Franciscan traveller William of Rubruck described Mongols making it in the thirteenth century, and it is still served at the Naadam festival and offered to guests through the summer.
tongba: Tongba is the traditional drink of the Limbu people of eastern Nepal, and its name is really that of its vessel, a wooden or metal pot holding fermented finger millet. The millet is cooked, mixed with a starter the Limbu call khesung and left to ferment; at the table hot water is poured over it, left to steep and drawn up through a straw with a filtered tip. Offering tongba is a mark of respect to a guest, sharing it is part of the Limbu wedding ceremony set out in the Mundhum, and it is also drunk in Sikkim and Darjeeling.
kopstootje: A kopstoot or kopstootje, a little head-butt, is a Dutch pairing rather than a mix: a small tulip glass of young jenever beside a glass of beer. Jenever is the juniper spirit of the Low Countries from which English gin descends, and it is traditionally poured so full that it bulges above the rim, so the first sip is taken by bending to the glass without lifting it, a bow that is itself called a kopstootje. No one is credited with the pairing.
l-and-p-and-vodka: Vodka topped with L&P, the lemony soft drink that began with mineral water from a spring at Paeroa, is an informal New Zealand mix with no recorded inventor or date.
macua: The Macuá was chosen as Nicaragua's national drink in October 2006, in a contest sponsored by the rum maker Flor de Caña with tourism businesses and backed by the national tourism institute. The winning recipe of white rum with guava and lemon was the work of Edmundo Miranda Sáenz, a paediatrician from Granada, who perfected it with his family, and a separate round of the contest named it after the pájaro macuá, a tropical bird of Nicaragua. The newspaper El Nuevo Diario criticised the rule that entries contain at least half Flor de Caña rum.
palm-wine: Palm wine is among the oldest drinks of West Africa, made wherever oil, raffia or coconut palms grow, and no one can say when it began. Tappers cut into the tree or its flower stalk and collect the sap, which starts fermenting within hours on its own wild yeasts. It goes by many names, emu in Yoruba and nsafufuo in Twi among them, it is distilled into spirits such as Ghana's akpeteshie and Nigeria's ogogoro, and it gave its name to palm wine music, the guitar style of the bars where it was sold, which helped shape highlife.
karsk: Karsk is coffee laced with spirit, traditionally home-distilled, and though its exact origin is unknown it was popular in Sweden's Bohuslän in the early nineteenth century and spread across Norway later that century, taking deepest root in Trøndelag. Its name comes from the Old Norse karskr, vigorous or lively. Elsewhere the same drink is kaffedoktor or knikt in parts of Norway and kask or kaffekask in Sweden, and in Trøndelag it remains a fixture of rural life.
seco-con-leche: Seco con leche, Panama's Seco Herrerano poured over ice with cold milk, is a country habit of Panama's interior with no credited inventor or recorded first glass.
cana-con-ruda: Caña con ruda is less a drink than a rite: every 1 August, Paraguayans take a little cane spirit steeped with rue and lemon, traditionally on an empty stomach, to keep away the misfortunes of August, the harsh tail end of winter. The custom is traced to Guaraní tradition, later remade with ingredients that came with the Spanish, rue from the Mediterranean and cane spirit from the sugar plantations. In Paraguay it is also called carrulim, from caña, ruda and limón, the national culture secretariat has declared it intangible cultural heritage, and the custom is shared in Argentina and Uruguay.
clerico: Clericó is the Río de la Plata's version of claret cup, the wine-and-fruit punch that was hugely popular in nineteenth-century Britain, and its name is a Spanish rendering of the English. Claret cup faded in English-speaking countries, but clericó lives on as a tradition in Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay, made with wine and plenty of chopped fruit and left to chill. Because Christmas and New Year fall in high summer there, it became a drink of those holidays, and in Paraguay it is often eaten with a spoon from the glass.
algarrobina: The algarrobina cocktail takes its name from its key ingredient, a dark syrup boiled down from the pods of the algarrobo tree of Peru's northern coast, mixed with pisco and milk, and no one is credited with first making it.
capitan: The capitán, pisco and red vermouth stirred over ice, is a classic Peruvian aperitif, and its origin is told two ways. A popular story credits army officers posted in the cold southern highlands around Puno, the captains of the name, with cutting their pisco with vermouth, while Peruvian sources tie its appearance in the first half of the twentieth century to Italian immigrants and the vermouth they brought into fashion. Neither names an inventor, and an old Lima marinera, the coastal song and dance, pays tribute to it.
chilcano: The chilcano goes back at least to the start of the twentieth century: Eudocio Carrera Vergara's account of a Lima jarana, a festive party, around 1900 is among the oldest references to it. Peruvian sources see it as an adaptation of the gin and ginger ale of the day, with pisco in place of gin, and it shares its name with chilcano de pescado, a fish broth, though how the drink came to borrow it is not recorded. It lost ground, returned in the 1950s and has since become one of Peru's most popular pisco drinks, with its own Semana del Chilcano each January.
machu-picchu: The Machu Picchu is a tall layered drink of Cusco's bars, built in green, yellow and red bands and named for the Inca citadel, and no one has documented who first made it.
gin-pom: Gin pom, Ginebra San Miguel mixed with water, ice and a sachet of powdered pomelo drink, is an everyday Filipino way with gin that no one is credited with starting.
weng-weng: The Weng Weng is a strong mixed drink of the beach bars of Boracay in the central Philippines, and nobody has documented who first mixed it or why it carries its name.
mad-dog: Wściekły pies, mad dog, is a Polish bar shot of chilled vodka over raspberry syrup with a few drops of Tabasco, and no one has documented who first poured it or named it.
tatanka: Bison grass vodka with cloudy apple juice is known in Poland as szarlotka, after the apple cake, and abroad as Tatanka, the Lakota word for the bison, but who first mixed it is not recorded.
nikita: The nikita, or niquita, comes from the fishing town of Câmara de Lobos on Madeira, where Portuguese sources credit a group of local friends with first blending ice cream, pineapple and sugar with white wine, beer or both. Its name is usually linked to Elton John's song Nikita, a hit in 1985, around the time the drink appeared. It is mixed until creamy with the same wooden stick used for poncha, and it has spread from Câmara de Lobos across Madeira and Porto Santo.
poncha: Poncha is Madeira's own drink, aguardente de cana, the island's sugar-cane spirit, mixed with honey or sugar and lemon juice, and Câmara de Lobos, the fishing town west of Funchal, is its traditional home. Its name is usually linked to punch, though the connection is not documented, and no one is credited with the first. It is mixed in the jug with a wooden stick with a ridged head, spun between the palms and known locally by the cheeky name caralhinho, and fishermen are said to have made it before setting out on cold mornings.
porto-tonico: Porto tónico, white port with tonic over ice, has become a signature aperitif of Porto as the port houses championed it to win white port new drinkers, though no one has a documented claim to the first.
bili: Bilí is a speciality of Vieques, the island off Puerto Rico's east coast: rum, traditionally the home-distilled pitorro, steeped with quenepas, the small green fruit also called Spanish lime, along with sugar and spice. No one is credited with the first batch, and recipes are passed down within Vieques families. Quenepas ripen in summer, and the bottles are often put away to rest for months, much as pitorro itself was traditionally buried to mature, and bilí remains closely tied to the island's identity.
chichaito: Chichaíto is a Puerto Rican shot of two ingredients, rum, often home-made pitorro, and anisette, served very cold, and no one is credited with inventing or naming it. It belongs to the island's long Christmas season, which runs into January and the Fiestas de la Calle San Sebastián, and to the parrandas, when friends arrive at a house late at night with guitars, güiros and songs and move on from door to door. A cold bottle waiting in the freezer is part of the welcome.
coco-loco: The coco loco, crazy coconut, is rum and coconut cream mixed in a freshly opened green coconut and drunk from the shell, a beach serve found across the Caribbean and Latin America that no one is credited with naming.
tuica-fiarta: Țuică is Romania's plum brandy, much of it distilled in village households, and țuică fiartă, boiled țuică, is its winter form. Sugar is first caramelised in a pot, then the țuică goes in with black peppercorns and is warmed until it steams, the caramel giving it its amber colour. No one is credited with the recipe, which belongs to cold days in the countryside and gatherings around Christmas, and in Transylvania and Maramureș the stronger plum spirit called pălincă or horincă is warmed the same way.
sbiten: Sbiten is one of the oldest drinks of the Eastern Slavs, a hot brew of honey, water, spices and herbs first mentioned in a Russian chronicle in the twelfth century and given a recipe in the sixteenth-century household manual Domostroy. For centuries it was a winter drink of every class, sold on the streets by sbitenshchiki whose heated kettle, the sbitennik, is counted among the ancestors of the samovar, until tea and coffee pushed it aside in the nineteenth century. Sbiten itself is usually alcohol-free, and the spiked version is made with wine or spirit.
yorsh: Yorsh, beer and vodka in one glass, takes its Russian name from the ruffe, a small spiny freshwater fish, and the mix has no recorded inventor or first use of the name.
bambus: Bambus, red wine mixed with cola, is a staple of bars and summer parties across the former Yugoslavia, and no one has documented who first made it or why it is called bamboo.
tatratea-hot: Tatratea Hot serves Slovakia's bottled tea liqueur, named for the High Tatras, warm with honey and lemon, a serve that has no recorded inventor.
dom-pedro: The Dom Pedro, vanilla ice cream blended with whisky, coffee liqueur or Amarula, is a South African after-dinner fixture, but no one has documented who first made one or where the name came from.
klippies-en-coke: Klippies en Coke, Klipdrift brandy with cola, is one of South Africa's most familiar brandy serves, and no one is credited with the first glass.
springbokkie: The springbokkie, little springbok in Afrikaans, is a South African shot in the green and gold of the national rugby team, crème de menthe under Amarula, and no one has documented who first poured it.
makgeolli: Makgeolli is often called Korea's oldest alcoholic drink, a cloudy, lightly sparkling brew of rice fermented with nuruk, a starter cake of wild yeasts and moulds, and its name is usually read as just strained. Long the farmers' drink, it earned the name nongju, farmers' wine. The twentieth century was hard on it, as colonial rule curbed home brewing and rice shortages later led the government to ban rice in brewing for years, so it was made with wheat, but it has since enjoyed a strong revival, often paired with savoury pancakes on rainy days.
somaek: Somaek is a contraction of soju and maekju, the Korean word for beer, and it is South Korea's best-known mixed drink, poured at hoesik, the after-work company dinners, and at gatherings of friends. It belongs to the wider Korean family of poktanju, bomb drinks, in which a spirit is mixed into beer, and nobody is credited with the first one; every table seems to have its own preferred proportion.
yogurt-soju: Yogurt soju, soju shaken with a sweet cultured milk drink such as Yakult and lemon-lime soda, is a recent Korean bar and restaurant mix that no one is credited with inventing.
agua-de-valencia: Agua de Valencia was first made in 1959 by Constante Gil at the Café Madrid in Valencia. According to the writer María Ángeles Arazo, a group of Basque visitors used to order agua de Bilbao, their name for the bar's best cava, and one day challenged Gil to offer them something new, so he mixed cava with Valencian orange juice, gin and vodka. For a decade it was known only to a small circle of regulars, and only in the 1970s did it spread into the city's wider nightlife.
leche-de-pantera: Leche de pantera, panther's milk, is a cold mix of gin with condensed or fresh milk, sometimes with egg white and cinnamon, and Spanish sources tie it to the Spanish Legion, whose members made it popular in the bars and taverns they frequented. Its exact origin is undocumented and no one is credited with inventing it. It was at its most popular in Spain in the years around the end of the Franco era and lives on as a curiosity of older bars.
queimada: Queimada is often called Celtic, but the prehistorian Carlos Alonso del Real pointed out that the still and the sugar it needs rule that out. Burnt aguardiente with sugar and coffee was known in Galicia by the early twentieth century, and the ritual as performed today took shape around the 1950s, when Galicians living away from home began making it at gatherings; the potter Tito Freire of Mondoñedo was making the footed clay bowls now used for it by 1955. The famous conxuro, the spell against the meigas, was written in Vigo in 1967 by Mariano Marcos Abalo.
rebujito: Rebujito, from the Andalusian rebujar, to mix together, is manzanilla or fino sherry lengthened with lemon-lime soda, and it belongs to the spring fairs and pilgrimages of western Andalusia, Seville's Feria de Abril, the Feria del Caballo in Jerez and El Rocío among them. It sits in a long tradition of wine regions stretching their everyday wines with something cool, and the English sherry cobbler is sometimes named as a forerunner. Nobody is credited with inventing it, and it became known beyond western Andalusia towards the end of the twentieth century.
sol-y-sombra: Sol y sombra, sun and shade, is usually said to take its name from the bullring, where seats are sold as sol, in the sun, sombra, in the shade, or sol y sombra, those that start in sunshine and fall into shadow as the afternoon goes on. The drink matches the idea with dark brandy for the shade and clear anís for the sun, served in a small glass. It is an old and widespread Spanish bar order with no known inventor or date, usually taken with coffee or after a meal.
vermut: Vermouth came to Spain from Turin in the nineteenth century, and Catalonia took to it so thoroughly that Reus, near Tarragona, became a centre of Spanish vermouth-making. Out of that grew fer el vermut, doing the vermouth: a late-morning ritual, above all on Sundays and holidays, of red vermouth over ice with an olive and a slice of orange, often with a splash of soda and a plate of tinned seafood or crisps before lunch. Older bars pour it from the tap, and the habit, which faded in the late twentieth century, has come back strongly in Barcelona.
arrack-and-ginger-beer: Ceylon arrack, distilled from coconut flower sap, with ginger beer and a squeeze of lime has become Sri Lanka's standing highball, though no one is credited with first mixing the two.
glogg: Glögg takes its name from glödgat vin, heated wine, and hot spiced wine has been drunk in the Nordic countries since at least the sixteenth century. Drinking glögg at Christmas became a Swedish tradition in the nineteenth century, made at home or bought from wine merchants whose bottles carried fanciful labels with tomte, and it spread to Finland at the end of that century. Since the twentieth century it has been served with almonds and raisins in the cup, alongside gingerbread and saffron buns.
grogg: Grogg is the Swedish word for a spirit topped up with a soft drink or soda, and it descends from grog, the watered rum of the Royal Navy. Admiral Edward Vernon, nicknamed Old Grog for his coat of grogram cloth, ordered in the middle of the eighteenth century that his sailors' rum be diluted with water, and the nickname passed to the mix. In Sweden the word travelled far from rum: a grogg can be vodka with lemon soda or whisky with ginger ale, and the mixers themselves are known as groggvirke, grogg timber.
kafi-fertig: Kafi fertig, finished coffee, is the coffee and schnapps of Central Switzerland, a farmhouse and village-inn drink of Lucerne and the surrounding cantons. A measure of fruit spirit, often Träsch distilled from pears and apples, or plum spirit or kirsch, goes into thin, sweetened coffee served in a glass. It goes by many local names, among them Kafi Luz in Lucerne and Kafi Zwetschgen or Kafi Träsch after the spirit, and no one is credited with the first.
boba-cocktail: The boba cocktail spikes Taiwanese bubble tea, milk tea with tapioca pearls, with rum or another spirit, a recent bar idea that no single bar is credited with.
konyagi-and-tonic: Konyagi, Tanzania's best-known locally made spirit, with tonic and a wedge of lime has become its standard long serve, though no one is credited with the pairing.
thai-bucket: The Thai bucket, a small plastic bucket of local spirit, mixer and ice to share, grew up on Thailand's backpacker beaches, above all at Haad Rin on Ko Pha-ngan, and no one is credited with the first.
sorrel: Sorrel is the Caribbean name for roselle, Hibiscus sabdariffa, a plant of African origin whose crimson calyces are steeped to make the drink, and it is thought to have reached the islands with the slave trade. The plant flowers as the days shorten, so its calyces come in around December, which is why sorrel became the Christmas drink of the English-speaking Caribbean, from Trinidad and Tobago to Jamaica. It is steeped with ginger, clove and orange peel, sweetened and often laced with rum, and its relatives include bissap in West Africa and agua de jamaica in Mexico.
boukha-and-orange: Boukha, Tunisia's dry fig spirit, lengthened with fresh orange juice over ice is a standard long serve in Tunisia, and no one is credited with the pairing.
aslan-sutu: Aslan sütü, lion's milk, is the Turkish nickname for rakı mixed with cold water, the way it is nearly always drunk, and no one knows who first called it that. Rakı is grape spirit distilled with aniseed, and water turns it milky white as the anise oils come out of solution, the effect known in English as the louche. It belongs to the long meyhane tradition of Istanbul and the Aegean, where it is sipped slowly over meze and conversation, and the usual advice is water first and ice after.
waragi-and-tonic: Uganda Waragi, the country's bottled, juniper-flavoured spirit, with tonic and lime is a usual serve in Kampala's bars, a pairing that no one is credited with.
horilka-z-pertsem: Horilka is the Ukrainian word for vodka and strong spirits, related to the verb hority, to burn, and horilka z pertsem is horilka bottled with whole chilli peppers, the style best known outside Ukraine. With honey added it becomes medova z pertsem, honey and pepper horilka. Families have long made it at home, commercial brands such as Nemiroff carried it abroad, and it is traditionally drunk cold with a meal, often with salo, cured pork fat, on dark rye bread.
angel-face: The Angel Face appeared in print in 1930 in The Savoy Cocktail Book, compiled by Harry Craddock at the American Bar of the Savoy Hotel in London: equal parts of gin, apricot brandy and calvados, shaken. The book gives no story or author for it, and none has turned up since. It is one of many balanced equal-parts drinks of the era, and it is on the International Bartenders Association's official list today among the Unforgettables.
atholl-brose: Atholl brose takes its name from Atholl, the Highland district of Perthshire, and from brose, the Scots word for oatmeal mixed with liquid. Legend credits the Earl of Atholl, who in 1475 is said to have put down a rebellion by the Lord of the Isles by filling a well with oatmeal, honey and whisky and capturing the rebel leader as he drank from it, though whisky is not recorded in Scotland until later. The drink itself, oatmeal water mixed with honey, whisky and often cream, is a festive Scottish recipe, and the name is also used for the dessert cranachan.
black-velvet: The usual story dates the Black Velvet to 1861, when Prince Albert, Queen Victoria's consort, died in December and a steward at Brooks's Club in London decided that even the champagne should be in mourning, mixing it with stout. Its black and white were said to echo the mourning bands of the time, but the drink long outlived its occasion. When cider stands in for the champagne it is known as the poor man's black velvet.
bucks-fizz: Buck's Fizz is named after Buck's Club in London, the gentlemen's club founded by Captain Herbert Buckmaster after the First World War, where it is said to have been first served in 1921 by the barman Malachy 'Pat' McGarry, who appears in P. G. Wodehouse's stories. The classic proportion is two parts champagne to one of orange juice, and the club's own recipe is said to hold extra ingredients. The Mimosa, credited to the Ritz in Paris a few years later, is essentially the same drink, and in Britain Buck's Fizz is a fixture of weddings and Christmas mornings.
